problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.

feedback.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is ${e}^{x/2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=1\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041958/assets/0dd98b517e2ed800f12a3672d2d6f45021f7f502cfe98c1e9308e52c05ab5f38.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${e}^{x/2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={e}^{x/2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{x/2}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{e}^{x/2}+C.
$$

Now, since  $v=\sqrt{5}\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{5})^{2} & =2{e}^{0/2}+C \\ \frac{5}{2} & =2+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{x/2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{x/2}+1 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4{e}^{x/2}+1}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4{e}^{1/2}+1} \\ v & =\sqrt{4\sqrt{e}+1} \\  & ≈2.8\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.
